q⁡(τ)=τ​𝔼​[s′​(τ​g)]=𝔼⁡[s⁡(τ​g)​g].q(\tau)=\tau\mathbb{E}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)]=\mathbb{E}[s(\tau g)g].

We first prove monotonicity. Differentiating q⁡(τ)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(τ​g)​g]q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s(\tau g)g] gives

q′​(τ)=𝔼⁡[s′​(τ​g)​g2].q^{\prime}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)g^{2}].

Since s′​(a)=1(ea/2+e−a/2)2>0s^{\prime}(a)=\frac{1}{(e^{a/2}+e^{-a/2})^{2}}>0 for every a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}, and since ℙ⁡(g≠0)=1\mathbb{P}(g\neq 0)=1, we have

q′​(τ)=𝔼⁡[s′​(τ​g)​g2]>0q^{\prime}(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s^{\prime}(\tau g)g^{2}]>0

for every τ≥0\tau\geq 0. Hence qq is strictly increasing on [0,∞)[0,\infty).

Next,

q⁡(0)=0⋅m⁡(0)=0.q(0)=0\cdot m(0)=0.

For the limit as τ→∞\tau\to\infty, using again the representation

q⁡(τ)=𝔼⁡[s⁡(τ​g)​g],q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[s(\tau g)g],

we note that for every g≠0g\neq 0,

s(τg)→𝟏{g>0}as τ→∞.s(\tau g)\to\mathbf{1}_{\{g>0\}}\qquad\text{as ~}\tau\to\infty.

Moreover, we have |s⁡(τ​g)​g|≤|g||s(\tau g)g|\leq|g| and 𝔼​|g|<∞\mathbb{E}|g|<\infty. Thus, by dominated convergence,

limτ→∞q(τ)=𝔼[g𝟏{g>0}]=12​π∫0∞xe−x2/2dx=12​π.\lim_{\tau\to\infty}q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[g\mathbf{1}_{\{g>0\}}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}xe^{-x^{2}/2}\,dx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.

Since qq is continuous and strictly increasing from 00 to 1/2​π1/\sqrt{2\pi}, it admits an inverse on (0,12​π).\left(0,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right). ∎

Lemma 22.

Let q⁡(τ)q(\tau) be defined as in Lemma 15. For every τ≥1/2\tau\geq 1/2,

12​π−q⁡(τ)≍1τ2.\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-q(\tau)\asymp\frac{1}{\tau^{2}}.

1−(s⁡(τ​x)−s⁡(−τ​x))=1−(2​s​(τ​x)−1)=2​(1−s⁡(τ​x))=21+eτ​x.1-\big(s(\tau x)-s(-\tau x)\big)=1-(2s(\tau x)-1)=2(1-s(\tau x))=\frac{2}{1+e^{\tau x}}.

Hence

12​π−q⁡(τ)=2​∫0∞x​ϕ​(x)1+eτ​x​𝑑x.\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-q(\tau)=2\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x\phi(x)}{1+e^{\tau x}}\,dx.

ϕ⁡(u/τ)≤ϕ⁡(0)=12​π,\phi(u/\tau)\leq\phi(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}},

12​π−q⁡(τ)≤2​ϕ​(0)τ2​∫0∞u1+eu​𝑑u≤Cτ2.\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-q(\tau)\leq\frac{2\phi(0)}{\tau^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{u}{1+e^{u}}\,du\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{2}}.

For the lower bound, restrict the integral to u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. Since τ≥1/2\tau\geq 1/2, we have u/τ≤2u/\tau\leq 2 for u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]. Thus

ϕ⁡(u/τ)≥ϕ⁡(2)>0for ​0≤u≤1.\phi(u/\tau)\geq\phi(2)>0\qquad\text{for }0\leq u\leq 1.

Therefore,

12​π−q⁡(τ)≥2​ϕ​(2)τ2​∫01u1+eu​𝑑u≥cτ2.\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}-q(\tau)\geq\frac{2\phi(2)}{\tau^{2}}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{u}{1+e^{u}}\,du\geq\frac{c}{\tau^{2}}.

Combining the two bounds proves the claim. ∎

Lemma 23.

Under Assumptions 1–2, we have

v=𝔼⁡[yi​xi]=q⁡(‖θ∗‖2)​θ∗‖θ∗‖2,v=\mathbb{E}[y_{i}x_{i}]=q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}},

where q⁡(τ):=𝔼g∼N⁡(0,1)​[s⁡(τ​g)​g].q(\tau):=\mathbb{E}_{g\sim N(0,1)}[s(\tau g)g]. Note that by Stein’s identity q⁡(τ)=𝔼⁡[τ​s′​(τ​g)]q(\tau)=\mathbb{E}[\tau s^{\prime}(\tau g)] and thus coincides with the definition in Lemma 15.

Proof.

By conditioning on xix_{i},

𝔼⁡[yi​xi]=𝔼⁡[s⁡(xi⊤​θ∗)​xi].\mathbb{E}[y_{i}x_{i}]=\mathbb{E}[s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*})x_{i}].

If θ∗=0\theta^{*}=0, the claim is immediate since the expectation is zero. Assume θ∗≠0\theta^{*}\neq 0 and set e:=θ∗‖θ∗‖2.e:=\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}. By rotational invariance of the standard Gaussian distribution, 𝔼⁡[s⁡(xi⊤​θ∗)​xi]\mathbb{E}[s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*})x_{i}] must be parallel to θ∗\theta^{*}, and its component along ee is

⟨𝔼⁡[s⁡(xi⊤​θ∗)​xi],e⟩=𝔼⁡[s⁡(‖θ∗‖2​g)​g]=q⁡(‖θ∗‖2),\left\langle\mathbb{E}[s(x_{i}^{\top}\theta^{*})x_{i}],e\right\rangle=\mathbb{E}[s(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}g)g]=q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}),

where g=xi⊤​e∼N⁡(0,1)g=x_{i}^{\top}e\sim N(0,1). Hence 𝔼⁡[yi​xi]=q⁡(‖θ∗‖2)​e=q⁡(‖θ∗‖2)​θ∗‖θ∗‖2.\mathbb{E}[y_{i}x_{i}]=q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})e=q(\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}. ∎

Appendix E Estimator in [26] and Algorithm 2

In this small appendix we provide more details on the estimator of [26], in order to support Equation (11) and Lemma 1 in the main text.

E.1 Sub-Gradient Descent

We first explain that Equation (11), or equivalently

r~t+1=r^t−2​πn​∑i=1n(sign⁡(xi⊤​r^t)+12−yi)​xi,\displaystyle\tilde{r}_{t+1}=\hat{r}_{t}-\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(\frac{\sign(x_{i}^{\top}\hat{r}_{t})+1}{2}-y_{i}\big)x_{i}, (97)
r^t+1=r~t+1‖r~t+1‖2\displaystyle\hat{r}_{t+1}=\frac{\tilde{r}_{t+1}}{\|\tilde{r}_{t+1}\|_{2}} (98)

as written in Lemma 1, can be viewed as a (sub-)gradient descent algorithm with respect to the ReLU loss. To see this, we transition to the {−1,1}\{-1,1\}-valued responses y~i=2​yi−1\tilde{y}_{i}=2y_{i}-1, consider the Hamming distance loss

Lham​(u)=1n​∑i=1n𝟏​(yi~≠sign⁡(xi⊤​u))=1n​∑i=1n𝟏​(−y~i​xi⊤​u≥0)L_{\rm ham}(u)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\big(\tilde{y_{i}}\neq\sign(x_{i}^{\top}u)\big)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\big(-\tilde{y}_{i}x_{i}^{\top}u\geq 0\big)

and then consider its convex relaxation, the ReLU loss obtained by replacing 𝟏​(a>0)\mathbf{1}(a>0) to ReLU⁡(a)=max⁡{a,0}=a+|a|2{\rm ReLU}(a)=\max\{a,0\}=\frac{a+|a|}{2},

LReLU​(u)=12​n​∑i=1n(|xi⊤​u|−y~i​xi⊤​u).L_{\rm ReLU}(u)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(|x_{i}^{\top}u|-\tilde{y}_{i}x_{i}^{\top}u\Big).

It is easy to see that a sub-gradient of the ReLU loss is given by

∂LReLU​(u)=12​n​∑i=1n(sign⁡(xi⊤​u)−y~i)​xi=1n​∑i=1n(sign⁡(xi⊤​u)+12−yi)​xi.\partial L_{\rm ReLU}(u)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\sign(x_{i}^{\top}u)-\tilde{y}_{i}\Big)x_{i}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\frac{\sign(x_{i}^{\top}u)+1}{2}-y_{i}\Big)x_{i}.

As such, (97) is exactly the sub-gradient descent with ReLU loss. Moreover, the additional normalization step, (98), is natural since the desired true direction θ∗/‖θ∗‖2\theta^{*}/\|\theta^{*}\|_{2} resides in 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}.

We show the derivation of Lemma 1 from Corollary 7 and Theorem 5 of [26] with the sparsity level kk therein set as dd. To start, we note that β\beta in [26] denotes the signal norm ‖θ∗‖2\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}. Hence β≥1\beta\geq 1 under Assumption 2.

We first show that (9) follows from the error rate of [26, Corollary 7]. In particular, Equation (17) therein shows that, to achieve ϵ\epsilon estimation error, we require a sample size of

n=Ω~​(dϵ2​‖θ∗‖2),if ​1≤‖θ∗‖2≤C0ϵ;\displaystyle n=\tilde{\Omega}\bigg(\frac{d}{\epsilon^{2}\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}\bigg),\qquad\textrm{if ~}1\leq\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\leq\frac{C_{0}}{\epsilon}; (99)
n=Ω~​(dϵ),if ​‖θ∗‖2>C0ϵ.\displaystyle n=\tilde{\Omega}\bigg(\frac{d}{\epsilon}\bigg),\qquad\textrm{if ~}\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}>\frac{C_{0}}{\epsilon}. (100)

This implies an error rate of

ϵ0=O~​(dn​‖θ∗‖2+dn)\epsilon_{0}=\tilde{O}\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{d}{n\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}}+\frac{d}{n}\bigg)

under any ‖θ∗‖2≥1\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}\geq 1, as with our Equation (9).

We then show the probability of 1−e−n1-e^{-n} and the iteration complexity of log2⁡log2​nd\log_{2}\log_{2}\frac{n}{d}, as stated in our Lemma 1. In fact, we can set ρ\rho of [26, Theorem 5], the probability parameter therein, as e−ne^{-n}. In view of Equation (14) therein, this can only add factor of polylog⁡(n)\polylog(n) to the sample complexity, which remains at n≳d​polylog⁡nn\gtrsim d\polylog n, as assumed in our Lemma 1. Moreover, in view of Equation (16) of [26], the sequence of direction estimates {r^t}t≥0\{\hat{r}_{t}\}_{t\geq 0} achieves a very fast convergence rate,

‖r^t−θ∗‖θ∗‖2‖2≤22−t​ϵ01−2−t,∀t≥0.\bigg\|\hat{r}_{t}-\frac{\theta^{*}}{\|\theta^{*}\|_{2}}\bigg\|_{2}\leq 2^{2^{-t}}\epsilon_{0}^{1-2^{-t}},\qquad\forall t\geq 0.

A direct calculation then finds that r^t\hat{r}_{t} with t≥log2⁡log2​ndt\geq\log_{2}\log_{2}\frac{n}{d} already achieves the desired direction estimation error of O~​(ϵ0)\tilde{O}(\epsilon_{0}).

E.3 Numerical Performance of Algorithm 2

We compare the estimation performance of Algorithm 2 with GD under the following settings:

  • •

    We set T0=30T_{0}=30 in Algorithm 2 and run it without sample splitting — i.e., both Step 1 and Step 2 use all the nn samples.

  • •

    We run GD in Algorithm 1 with θ0=0\theta_{0}=0, η=4\eta=4 for 400400 iterations. Suppose that the MLE exists, then traditional optimization theory [31] guarantees that the GD iterates converge to MLE, and as we run sufficiently many iterations we expect that the estimator, θ400\theta_{400}, well approximates MLE.

Consistent with Remark 4, our numerical simulations suggest that Algorithm 2 outperforms GD, and possibly also MLE, in high-dimensional setting, especially when nn is only moderately large. We provide two numerical examples to illustrate this phenomenon:

  • •

    We first test both algorithms in a high-dimensional regime with (d,‖θ∗‖2)=(1000,2)(d,\|\theta^{*}\|_{2})=(1000,2) and n∈{3000,5000,8000,10000,15000,20000,30000}n\in\{3000,5000,8000,10000,15000,20000,30000\}. The log-log plots in Figure 2(a) suggest that Algorithm 2 yields more accurate estimates than GD when n<10000n<10000, while GD becomes slightly better when n>10000n>10000. The reference dashed line further confirms the O(n−1/2)O(n^{-1/2}) error decay rate of Algorithm 2.

  • •

    We next consider the setting (n,d)=(5000,1000)(n,d)=(5000,1000) and vary ‖θ∗‖2\|\theta^{*}\|_{2} over {1,2,4,6,8}\{1,2,4,6,8\}. The results in Figure 2(b) again show that Algorithm 2 can substantially outperform GD in high-dimensional, moderate-sample regimes.
